title: New Method Pulls Faint Planets Out of Webb Images
paragraphs: Astronomers at Caltech and partner institutions have described a technique that squeezes more out of the James Webb Space Telescope's existing images. The central difficulty of photographing exoplanets is contrast: a planet can be billions of times fainter than its star, and the star's glare swamps it. The study, titled "Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit", appeared in Nature on 4 November 2026.

The approach, called FLIP (Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets), builds a digital twin of Webb's NIRCam camera and solves for millions of possible physical imperfections. The model then predicts the star's glare so it can be subtracted. A first attempt, training machine learning directly to predict starlight patterns, failed, so the team used machine-learning optimisation tools to model the physics instead. In tests on known planets, sensitivity was two to 15 times greater than with conventional approaches, and Caltech reports that FLIP revealed a planet in the 51 Eridani system that the original analysis had missed. Co-author Jason Wang said the team had gone beyond the telescope's stability limit for the first time.

Caveats remain. FLIP has been demonstrated only on Webb data, even though Webb is stable to the nanometre. Tests on the Roman Space Telescope and ground-based instruments are planned but not yet done, and imaging a truly Earth-like world is still a goal, not a result. Funders included the Space Telescope Science Institute, the Sloan Foundation, an Amazon AI4Science Discovery Award and the National Science Foundation.

questions.q: Why are exoplanets hard to photograph?
questions.a: They are far fainter than their stars, whose glare swamps them.

questions.q: What happened to the first attempt?
questions.a: Training machine learning to predict starlight failed.

questions.q: What has not been done yet?
questions.a: Tests on the Roman Space Telescope and ground-based instruments.
